slides.heading: The first leaders of the Congress
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **Early Nationalists**, also called the **Moderates**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: who the Early Nationalists were, their objectives and methods, the leaders Naoroji, Banerjee and Gokhale, and their achievements and limits
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: For about twenty years after eighteen eighty-five, the Indian National Congress was led by men we call the Early Nationalists, or Moderates. They were lawyers, teachers and journalists who believed that patient argument would win fair treatment for India. In this part we look at what they wanted, how they worked, three of their leaders, and what they achieved.

slides.heading: Two phases, two styles
slides.body_md: Moderates first; **Assertive Nationalists** after about 1905.

slides.narration: The national movement before the First World War had two phases. The Early Nationalists sought reforms within British rule and used petitions and appeals. After about nineteen hundred and five, the Assertive Nationalists demanded self-rule and used swadeshi, boycott and national education. Keep this chart in mind as we study each group in turn.

slides.heading: What the Moderates wanted
slides.body_md: Political, **administrative** and **economic** demands.

rows: Larger legislative councils with more elected Indians; freedom of speech and the Press
Civil service examination in India as well as England; higher age limit; separation of judiciary from executive
Lower land revenue; less military spending from Indian funds; protection of Indian industry

visual.alt: Table of Moderate demands: political (larger councils, free speech and Press), administrative (civil service examination in India, higher age limit, separate judiciary) and economic (lower land revenue, less military spending, protection of industry)
visual.caption: Demands of the Early Nationalists.

slides.narration: The Early Nationalists asked for larger legislative councils with more elected Indians, and for freedom of speech and the Press. They wanted the civil service examination held in India as well as England, so that more Indians could enter the higher services. And they asked for lower land revenue, less military spending from Indian funds and protection for Indian industry.

visual.alt: Worked example table sorting four imagined resolutions: civil service examination in Bombay is administrative, cutting war spending and reducing land tax are economic, and elected Indians in the councils is political

slides.narration: Let us sort four imagined resolutions. Holding the civil service examination in Bombay as well as London is about jobs, so it is administrative. Cutting the share of Indian revenue spent on frontier wars is about money, so it is economic. Allowing elected Indians into the councils is about power, so it is political. Reducing the land tax in famine years is economic.

slides.heading: How the Moderates worked
slides.body_md: **Petitions**, meetings, delegations, and faith in **British justice**.

visual.alt: Flow of Moderate methods: petitions and memoranda, public meetings and resolutions, delegations to Britain, and appeals to the British sense of justice
visual.caption: Prayers, petitions and protests.

slides.narration: The Moderates worked strictly within the law. They sent petitions and memoranda full of facts and figures. They held public meetings and passed resolutions to build opinion. They sent delegations to Britain to inform members of Parliament and voters. Behind all this was their belief that the British, once properly informed, would act justly.

slides.body_md: **Naoroji**, **Banerjee** and **Gokhale**.

slides.narration: Here are three leaders you must know. Dadabhai Naoroji set out the drain of wealth argument and was elected to the British House of Commons in eighteen ninety-two. Surendranath Banerjee founded the Indian Association and edited The Bengalee. Gopal Krishna Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society and criticised government budgets in the Imperial Legislative Council.

slides.narration: Dadabhai Naoroji, remembered as the Grand Old Man of India, worked largely in Britain, where he became the first Indian member of the House of Commons. He presided over the Congress three times. Surendranath Banerjee worked through public agitation: he toured India against a lower age limit for the civil service examination and used his newspaper to spread nationalist ideas.

slides.narration: Gopal Krishna Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society in nineteen hundred and five to train people for selfless public work, and in the same year presided over the Banaras session of the Congress. In the Imperial Legislative Council he examined budgets closely and argued for more spending on education. Mahatma Gandhi later looked upon him as his political guide.

slides.heading: A balanced appraisal
slides.body_md: They laid **foundations**, but **petitions** won little.

rows: Support mainly from the educated middle class
Too much faith in British justice
Some reforms, e.g. the Indian Councils Act, 1892

slides.narration: How should we judge the Moderates? They built an all-India platform, trained Indians in political work and exposed the economic exploitation of India. They also won some reforms, such as the Indian Councils Act of eighteen ninety-two. But their support came mainly from the educated middle class, and their faith in British justice brought only small gains.

bullets: **Moderates**, 1885 to about 1907: reforms **within** British rule.
Demands: **councils**, **services**, **economic** relief.

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: Moderates from 1885 to about 1907, demands for councils, services and economic reform, methods of petitions, meetings and delegations, the leaders Naoroji, Banerjee and Gokhale, and the foundation they laid
visual.caption: Part 1 in five lines.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. The Early Nationalists led the Congress from eighteen eighty-five to about nineteen hundred and seven. They wanted reforms within British rule and used petitions, meetings and delegations. Naoroji, Banerjee and Gokhale were their leading figures. Their gains were modest, but they laid the foundation on which later movements were built.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Do not say the Moderates wanted **complete independence**; they wanted reforms.
Give **two** contributions for each leader, with a **year** where you can.
Naoroji presided **three** times: **1886, 1893, 1906**.
For an appraisal, give **both** achievements and limitations.
slides.narration: Some tips. Never write that the Moderates demanded complete independence; they sought reforms within British rule. For each leader, give two contributions and a year where possible. Remember that Naoroji presided over the Congress three times. And when you are asked to assess the Moderates, give achievements as well as limitations.

goals: Explain the stated reason and the nationalist view of the Partition of Bengal, 1905
Give the reasons for the Surat Split of 1907
Compare the objectives and methods of the Assertive Nationalists with those of the Moderates

slides.heading: A sharper turn in the national movement
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **Partition of Bengal**, the **Surat Split** and **Lal, Bal and Pal**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the Partition of Bengal in 1905, the rise of the Assertive Nationalists, swadeshi, boycott and national education, the Surat Split of 1907, and the leaders Lal, Bal and Pal
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In nineteen hundred and five, a decision of the government set off the biggest protest India had yet seen. In this part we study the Partition of Bengal, the rise of a new group called the Assertive Nationalists, their methods of swadeshi, boycott and national education, the split in the Congress at Surat, and three leaders known together as Lal, Bal and Pal.

slides.heading: The Partition of Bengal, 1905
slides.body_md: Lord **Curzon**; effective **16 October 1905**.

rows: Bengal too large to govern efficiently
Divide and rule: weaken Bengali nationalism; divide Hindus and Muslims
Annulled 1911 (Delhi Durbar); capital moved to Delhi

visual.alt: Table of facts on the Partition of Bengal: under Lord Curzon, announced July 1905 and effective 16 October 1905; new province Eastern Bengal and Assam with capital Dacca; stated reason size; nationalist view divide and rule; annulled 1911 at the Delhi Durbar with the capital moved to Delhi

slides.narration: Under Lord Curzon, the large province of Bengal was divided. The partition took effect on the sixteenth of October, nineteen hundred and five. The eastern districts were joined with Assam to form a new province, Eastern Bengal and Assam, with its capital at Dacca. The government said Bengal was too large to govern well. Nationalists saw it very differently.

slides.heading: Stated reason and nationalist view
columns:
**Government's reason**

- Bengal **too large** and populous
- Better **administration**

**Nationalist view**

- **Divide and rule**
- Weaken **Bengali nationalism**
- Set **Hindus and Muslims** apart

rows: Bengal too large to govern efficiently
Divide and rule: weaken Bengali nationalism; divide Hindus and Muslims
Annulled 1911 (Delhi Durbar); capital moved to Delhi

visual.alt: Table of facts on the Partition of Bengal: under Lord Curzon, announced July 1905 and effective 16 October 1905; new province Eastern Bengal and Assam with capital Dacca; stated reason size; nationalist view divide and rule; annulled 1911 at the Delhi Durbar with the capital moved to Delhi

slides.narration: The government gave an administrative reason: Bengal was too large and populous to be governed efficiently. Nationalists believed the real aim was to divide and rule. Bengal was then the centre of nationalist activity, and creating a Muslim-majority province in the east, they argued, was meant to weaken that strength and set the two communities against each other.

slides.heading: How Bengal answered
slides.body_md: Mourning, **rakhis**, **swadeshi** and **boycott**.

nodes.label: 16 October: day of mourning and fasting
Rakhis tied as a sign of unity
Boycott of British goods and institutions

visual.alt: Flow of protest against the partition: a day of mourning on 16 October, rakhis as a sign of unity, swadeshi, boycott of British goods and institutions, and the spread of the movement beyond Bengal
visual.caption: How Bengal answered.

slides.narration: The day the partition took effect was observed as a day of mourning. Many families fasted and shops stayed closed. Hindus and Muslims tied rakhis on one another as a sign of unity. People took a pledge to use only Indian goods and to boycott British ones. Students and women joined in large numbers, and the movement spread beyond Bengal.

slides.heading: Why the Assertive Nationalists rose
slides.body_md: Failure of petitions, **Curzon's** policies, and new **confidence**.

visual.alt: Flow of causes of the rise of the Assertive Nationalists: petitions bring little, Curzon's policies and the partition, Japan's victory over Russia in 1905, growing confidence and anger, and the rise of the Assertive group
visual.caption: Why a new group rose.

slides.narration: Why did a new, more assertive group rise at this time? Twenty years of petitions had brought little. Lord Curzon's policies, above all the partition, showed that the government ignored Indian opinion. And in nineteen hundred and five Japan defeated Russia, showing that an Asian nation could defeat a European power. Confidence and anger grew together.

slides.heading: The Assertive methods
slides.body_md: **Swadeshi**, **boycott**, **national education**, **passive resistance**.

rows: Use goods made in India; support Indian industry
Refuse British goods, and also government schools, courts and titles
Schools and colleges run by Indians, outside government control
Peaceful refusal to obey unjust measures

visual.alt: Table of Assertive methods: swadeshi (use Indian goods), boycott (refuse British goods, schools, courts and titles), national education (Indian-run schools and colleges) and passive resistance (peaceful refusal to obey unjust measures)

slides.narration: The Assertive Nationalists demanded swaraj, or self-rule. Their methods were swadeshi, which meant using goods made in India; boycott of British goods, and later of government schools, courts and titles; national education in schools and colleges run by Indians; and passive resistance, the peaceful refusal to obey unjust measures. These methods let ordinary people take part.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: which method is it?
slides.body_md: Classify four imagined actions of **1906**.
bullets: Using or selling **Indian** goods: **swadeshi**.
Refusing **British** goods or institutions: **boycott**.
Building **Indian-run** schools: **national education**.

rows: A Pune shop sells only mill cloth from Indian mills
Students refuse to sit for a government college examination
A village teacher opens a school with lessons in Bengali on Indian history
Traders refuse to unload British salt and sugar

visual.alt: Worked example table classifying four imagined actions of 1906: selling only Indian mill cloth is swadeshi, refusing a government college examination and refusing to unload British goods are boycott, and a village school teaching Indian history is national education
visual.caption: Ask: is it using Indian, refusing British, or building Indian institutions?

slides.narration: Let us classify four imagined actions of nineteen hundred and six. A shop in Pune that sells only cloth from Indian mills is practising swadeshi. Students who refuse to sit a government college examination, and traders who refuse to unload British salt, are practising boycott. A village teacher who opens a school teaching Indian history in Bengali is building national education.

slides.heading: The Surat Split, 1907
slides.body_md: **Methods** and the **presidency** divided the Congress.

sections.heading: 1. The Early Nationalists: objectives and methods
sections.body_md:
- **Period:** 1885 to about 1905–07; also called the **Moderates**; mainly the **educated middle class**.
- **Objectives:** larger **legislative councils** with elected Indians; **Indianisation** of services (civil service examination in India too, higher age limit); separation of judiciary from executive; **economic** relief (lower land revenue, less military spending, protection of industry); civil rights (free speech and Press).
- **Methods:** **petitions** and memoranda, **public meetings** and resolutions, **delegations** to Britain; faith in the British **sense of justice** ("prayers, petitions and protests").
- **Achievements:** all-India platform; political training; exposure of **economic exploitation**; **Indian Councils Act, 1892**. **Limitations:** narrow base; small gains from petitions.

sections.heading: 3. The Partition of Bengal (1905)
sections.body_md:
- **Viceroy:** Lord **Curzon**; announced **July 1905**, effective **16 October 1905**.
- **New province:** **Eastern Bengal and Assam**, capital **Dacca**.
- **Stated reason:** Bengal too **large** to govern efficiently.
- **Nationalist view:** **divide and rule**, to weaken Bengali nationalism and divide Hindus and Muslims.
- **Protest:** day of **mourning**; **rakhis** as a symbol of unity; **swadeshi** and **boycott**; students and women took part.
- **Outcome:** annulled in **1911**, announced at the **Delhi Durbar**; capital moved from Calcutta to **Delhi**.

key_terms.definition_md: The division of Bengal by Lord Curzon, effective 16 October 1905; annulled in 1911.
A policy of keeping control by setting groups of the ruled against one another.

sections.heading: 4. The Surat Split (1907)
sections.body_md:
- **Background:** the **Calcutta session (1906)**, under Naoroji, adopted **swaraj**, **swadeshi**, **boycott** and **national education**.
- **Causes:** differences over **goals and methods**; fear that the Moderates would drop the 1906 resolutions; venue moved from **Nagpur** to **Surat**; dispute over the **presidency**: the Moderates backed **Rash Behari Ghosh**, the Assertive group wanted **Lala Lajpat Rai**.
- **Result:** the session broke up in **disorder** (December 1907); the Moderates kept control of the Congress; the government repressed Assertive leaders; the groups **reunited at Lucknow, 1916**.

sections.heading: 5. The Assertive Nationalists: objectives and methods
sections.body_md:
- **Causes of their rise:** failure of Moderate methods; **Curzon's** policies and the **partition**; **Japan's victory over Russia (1905)**; growing self-confidence.
- **Objectives:** **swaraj** (self-rule); **mass participation**; self-reliance and national pride.
- **Methods:** **swadeshi** (use Indian goods); **boycott** (of British goods, government schools, courts, titles); **national education** (Indian-run schools and colleges); **passive resistance** (peaceful refusal to obey unjust measures).
- **Contrast with the Moderates:** swaraj against reforms; mass action against petitions; lost faith in British justice.

sections.heading: 6. Tilak, Pal and Lajpat Rai
sections.body_md:
- **Bal Gangadhar Tilak** (Maharashtra): **Kesari** (Marathi) and **Mahratta** (English); **Ganapati** and **Shivaji** festivals; declared self-rule a **birthright** of Indians (paraphrased); imprisoned at **Mandalay, 1908–14**; started a **Home Rule League, 1916**.
- **Bipin Chandra Pal** (Bengal): English weekly **New India**; leading voice of **swadeshi** and **boycott**.
- **Lala Lajpat Rai** (Punjab): **Punjab Kesari**; linked with the **Arya Samaj** and education; **deported to Mandalay, 1907**. (Later context: injured during a protest against the Simon Commission in 1928; died soon after.)
- Together known as **Lal, Bal and Pal**.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying the Moderates wanted complete independence.
- Writing 1907 for the partition (it was 1905; Surat was 1907).
- Naming the wrong Viceroy: the partition was under **Curzon**.
- Mixing up the Moderate (Rash Behari Ghosh) and Assertive (Lajpat Rai) choices at Surat.
- Quoting Tilak's swaraj declaration inaccurately; describe the idea in your own words.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points (for a leader, two contributions).
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one point per mark; the 4-mark part often asks for causes and effects, a comparison or a balanced judgement.

questions.stem_md: In ICSE history, the phase of the Early Nationalists (Moderates) in the Indian National Congress is usually dated as
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1885 to 1905–07. The Early Nationalists led the Congress from its founding in 1885 until about 1905–07, when the Assertive Nationalists rose and the Congress split at Surat. The other periods belong to 1857, the Gandhian movements and the last phase of the freedom struggle.

questions.stem_md: Which demand of the Early Nationalists was aimed at the Indianisation of the higher services?

options.text_md: Complete independence from British rule at once
Boycott of all British schools and colleges
Abolition of the Indian National Congress
Holding the Indian Civil Service examination in India as well as in England

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Holding the Indian Civil Service examination in India as well as in England. Holding the civil service examination simultaneously in India (and raising the age limit) would let more Indians enter the higher services. Immediate independence and boycott were not Moderate demands, and they did not seek to abolish their own organisation.

questions.stem_md: Which set of methods best describes how the Early Nationalists pressed their demands?

options.text_md: Petitions, appeals and protest meetings within the law
Armed attacks on government offices
Mass non-payment of taxes all over India
Boycott of the legislative councils

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Petitions, appeals and protest meetings within the law. The Moderates used constitutional means: petitions and memoranda, appeals to British opinion and public meetings with resolutions. Violence, mass tax refusal and boycott of councils were not their methods.

questions.stem_md: Why did the Early Nationalists send delegations and memorials to Britain rather than organise mass protests in India?

options.text_md: They had no supporters at all in India
The British Parliament had banned all meetings in Britain
They believed that the British public and Parliament would grant justice once they knew the facts
They wanted to leave India permanently

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** They believed that the British public and Parliament would grant justice once they knew the facts. The Moderates had faith in the British sense of justice and fair play, so they tried to educate British opinion. They did have supporters in India, meetings in Britain were not banned, and they were not trying to emigrate.

questions.stem_md: An imagined resolution of an early Congress session asks the government to lower land revenue, to reduce the share of military spending paid from Indian funds, and to protect Indian industries. Which conclusion about the thinking behind it is best supported?

options.text_md: Its authors held that British rule must end at once before any economic recovery was possible
Its authors thought that economic policy was already fair and asked only for more jobs for educated Indians
Its authors held that existing economic policy was hurting India, but they believed that the remedy lay in asking the government to change that policy
Its authors wanted Indians to stop buying British goods until the demands were met

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Its authors held that existing economic policy was hurting India, but they believed that the remedy lay in asking the government to change that policy. The resolution criticises economic policy (revenue, military burden, neglect of industry) yet only asks the government to reform it, which fits the Moderate faith in constitutional pressure. It does not call for an end to British rule or for boycott (both Assertive ideas), and it would make no sense if policy were thought fair.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Moderate editor writes in 1893 that the enlarged councils are welcome: members may now discuss the budget, but they cannot vote on it and many seats are still filled by nomination. Which course of action would best fit his position?

options.text_md: Welcome the change, and keep asking by resolutions and petitions for more elected members and a real say over the budget
Boycott the councils and call on people to stop paying taxes until the budget is changed
Declare that the change proves the Congress has achieved its aims and should be closed
Give up constitutional methods and organise an armed rising, since the councils have no power

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Welcome the change, and keep asking by resolutions and petitions for more elected members and a real say over the budget. He sees the Act of 1892 as a step forward but an incomplete one, so a Moderate would press on with constitutional demands for more elected members and budget powers. Boycott and tax refusal belong to the Assertive phase, declaring victory ignores his own complaints, and armed rising was never a Moderate method.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Early Nationalists relied on petitions and appeals rather than direct confrontation with the government.

**Reason (R):** They believed that British rule, if properly informed, would treat Indians justly.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: their faith in British justice led them to use persuasion through petitions and appeals.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** From 1885 the Early Nationalists demanded complete independence from Britain.

**Reason (R):** The Early Nationalists wanted more Indians in the legislative councils and the higher services.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the Moderates sought reforms within British rule, not complete independence. R is true: expansion of councils and Indianisation of services were among their main demands.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Early Nationalists drew most of their support from peasants and industrial workers in the villages and mills.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Their support came mainly from the educated middle class in the towns, which is one reason critics said they lacked a mass base.

questions.stem_md: The methods of the Early Nationalists are often summed up as prayers, petitions and ___.
questions.solution_md: They are remembered as the method of prayers, petitions and protests (meetings and resolutions within the law).

questions.stem_md: State any two objectives of the Early Nationalists.
questions.solution_md: Any two Moderate objectives.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Expansion and reform of the legislative councils**, with more elected Indian members.
2. **Indianisation of the higher services**, for example by holding the civil service examination in India as well. (Also: lower land revenue, less military spending, freedom of the Press.)

questions.stem_md: Describe two methods the Early Nationalists used to win their demands.
questions.solution_md: Two constitutional methods described.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Petitions and memoranda** to the government, setting out grievances with facts and figures.
2. **Public meetings and resolutions** to build opinion, and **delegations** to Britain to inform British leaders and voters.

questions.stem_md: Why did many younger nationalists come to regard the methods of the Moderates as ineffective by about 1905?
questions.solution_md: Limited gains; government indifference shown by partition.

answer.model_answer_md: Twenty years of **petitions** had brought only small changes, such as the **Councils Act of 1892**, while many key demands were **ignored**. Measures like the **Partition of Bengal** convinced younger leaders that the government would not yield to **appeals** alone.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate the work of the Early Nationalists by stating three things they achieved despite their limited methods.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct achievements.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. They built an **all-India platform** and trained Indians in **political work** and public debate.
2. They exposed the **economic exploitation** of India, especially through the **drain of wealth** argument.
3. They won some reforms, such as the **Indian Councils Act of 1892**, and laid the base on which later, more assertive movements grew.

marking_scheme.step: Reforms or foundation for later movements

questions.stem_md: Which Indian leader was elected to the British House of Commons in 1892?

options.text_md: Gopal Krishna Gokhale
Bal Gangadhar Tilak
Bipin Chandra Pal
Dadabhai Naoroji

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Dadabhai Naoroji. Dadabhai Naoroji was elected to the House of Commons in 1892 and used his seat to raise Indian issues. Gokhale served in the Imperial Legislative Council in India; Tilak and Pal were Assertive leaders.

questions.stem_md: An imagined exhibition card says of a leader: "He explained India's poverty by the steady flow of wealth to Britain, and he won a seat in the British House of Commons." Why would a student of the Early Nationalists see these two achievements as fitting together?

options.text_md: The seat let him command the army and end British rule, which proved the drain argument
The seat let him put evidence of India's grievances before British lawmakers and public, whom the Moderates hoped to persuade
The two achievements show that he thought India's economy was doing well and needed no reform
The seat made him the organiser of the boycott of British goods in Bengal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The seat let him put evidence of India's grievances before British lawmakers and public, whom the Moderates hoped to persuade. The Moderates relied on persuading British opinion, so winning a place in the House of Commons gave Naoroji a platform to argue the drain of wealth where decisions were made. A Commons seat gave no command of the army, his argument says India was being impoverished, and the boycott was an Assertive method.

questions.stem_md: Dadabhai Naoroji presided over the Indian National Congress three times. In which set of years?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 1886, 1893 and 1906. He presided in 1886, 1893, 1906. The other sets mix in wrong years.

questions.stem_md: Surendranath Banerjee, along with Ananda Mohan Bose, founded which organisation in 1876?

options.text_md: The Servants of India Society
The Indian Association
The Home Rule League
The Arya Samaj

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Indian Association. The Indian Association of Calcutta was founded in 1876 by Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose. Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society, Tilak started a Home Rule League, and Dayananda founded the Arya Samaj.

questions.stem_md: In the late 1870s, an imagined young graduate in Lahore is refused entry to the civil service examination because he is just over the lowered age limit; the examination is held only in London, which his family cannot afford. Which pair of Early Nationalist demands, if granted, would most directly have removed both of his obstacles?

options.text_md: Lower land revenue, and protection for Indian industries
More elected Indian members in the councils, and the right to discuss the budget
A higher maximum age, and the examination held in India as well as in England
Freedom of the Press, and the right to hold public meetings

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A higher maximum age, and the examination held in India as well as in England. His two obstacles are the age limit and the London-only examination, which the Moderates answered with a demand for a higher age limit and simultaneous examinations in India. The other pairs are real Moderate demands but would not have helped him: they concern revenue and industry, the councils, and civil liberties.

questions.stem_md: Through which newspaper did Surendranath Banerjee spread nationalist ideas?

options.text_md: Kesari
New India
Mahratta
The Bengalee

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Bengalee. Banerjee edited The Bengalee. Kesari and Mahratta were Tilak's papers, and New India was linked with Bipin Chandra Pal.

questions.stem_md: Gopal Krishna Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society in which year?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1905. Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society in 1905 to train dedicated workers for public service. 1885 is the founding of the Congress, 1876 the Indian Association and 1916 the Home Rule Leagues.

questions.stem_md: Why were Gopal Krishna Gokhale's speeches in the Imperial Legislative Council important for the national movement?

options.text_md: He announced the boycott of British goods from the council floor
He was the Viceroy who presided over the council
He used facts and figures to criticise government spending and policy from inside the council
He moved the resolution that partitioned Bengal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** He used facts and figures to criticise government spending and policy from inside the council. As a member of the council, Gokhale examined budgets closely and criticised heavy military spending and the neglect of education with careful arguments. Boycott was an Assertive method, he was never Viceroy, and partition was the government's decision.

questions.stem_md: Which Moderate leader did Mahatma Gandhi regard as his political guide (guru)?

options.text_md: Dadabhai Naoroji
Gopal Krishna Gokhale
Surendranath Banerjee
Bipin Chandra Pal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Gopal Krishna Gokhale. Gandhi looked upon Gokhale as his political guru, a relationship widely described in Indian history. The other leaders were not described by Gandhi in this way.

questions.stem_md: Match each Early Nationalist leader with a contribution linked to him.

options.text_md: Dadabhai Naoroji
Surendranath Banerjee
Gopal Krishna Gokhale
A. O. Hume

match_right.text_md: Helped found the Indian National Congress, 1885
Set out the drain of wealth argument
Founded the Servants of India Society, 1905

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Naoroji: drain of wealth; Banerjee: Indian Association; Gokhale: Servants of India Society; Hume: founding of the Congress.

questions.stem_md: State two contributions of Dadabhai Naoroji to the national movement.
questions.solution_md: Any two contributions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He set out the **drain of wealth** argument in his book **Poverty and Un-British Rule in India**.
2. As a **member of the House of Commons (1892)** he raised Indian grievances in Britain; he was **Congress President** in 1886, 1893 and 1906.

questions.stem_md: State two contributions of Surendranath Banerjee.
questions.solution_md: Any two contributions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He founded the **Indian Association (1876)** with Ananda Mohan Bose and led an all-India campaign on the **civil service age limit**.
2. He spread nationalist ideas through his paper **The Bengalee** and led the protest against the **Partition of Bengal**.

questions.stem_md: State two contributions of Gopal Krishna Gokhale.
questions.solution_md: Any two contributions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He founded the **Servants of India Society (1905)** to train selfless workers for national service.
2. In the **Imperial Legislative Council** he criticised government budgets and pressed for **education** and lower **military spending**; he presided over the **Banaras session of 1905**.

questions.stem_md: Naoroji, Banerjee and Gokhale worked in different arenas. Name the main arena of each and one thing he achieved there.
questions.solution_md: Arena plus achievement for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Naoroji, British Parliament and writing:** raised Indian issues in the **House of Commons** and set out the **drain** argument.
2. **Banerjee, public agitation and the Press:** built the **Indian Association** and toured India on the **civil service** issue; edited **The Bengalee**.
3. **Gokhale, the legislative council:** criticised **budgets** with facts and figures, and trained workers through the **Servants of India Society**.

questions.stem_md: The Partition of Bengal of 1905 was carried out under which Viceroy?

options.text_md: Lord Curzon
Lord Ripon
Lord Lytton
Lord Minto

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Lord Curzon. Lord Curzon (Viceroy 1899–1905) carried out the partition. Ripon and Lytton came earlier, and Minto followed Curzon.

questions.stem_md: On which date did the Partition of Bengal come into effect?

options.text_md: 28 December 1885
16 October 1905
12 December 1911
1 April 1916

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 16 October 1905. The partition took effect on 16 October 1905, which was observed as a day of mourning. 28 December 1885 is the founding of the Congress, and 12 December 1911 is the Delhi Durbar at which the annulment was announced.

questions.stem_md: What was the official reason the government gave for partitioning Bengal?

options.text_md: Bengal had asked to be divided by a popular vote
The Congress had demanded the partition
Bengal needed a separate army
The province was too large and populous to be governed efficiently

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The province was too large and populous to be governed efficiently. The government said the province was too large to administer well. There was no popular vote, the Congress opposed the partition, and an army was not the reason.

questions.stem_md: Why did nationalists describe the Partition of Bengal as an example of "divide and rule"?

options.text_md: They believed it aimed to weaken Bengali nationalism and to divide Hindus and Muslims
They believed it would make Bengal richer than other provinces
They believed it would give Bengal its own Parliament
They believed it was meant to end famines in Bengal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** They believed it aimed to weaken Bengali nationalism and to divide Hindus and Muslims. Nationalists saw the partition as a way to break the political strength of Bengal, then the centre of nationalist activity, and to create a Muslim-majority province in the east, setting communities against each other. The other options are not the nationalist view.

questions.stem_md: The government said it divided Bengal in 1905 because the province was too large to govern well. A student wants to show from the shape of the new arrangement that the aim was also political. Which detail best supports her case?

options.text_md: The eastern districts were joined with Assam to form the province of Eastern Bengal and Assam
Dacca was made the capital of the new eastern province
The division created a Muslim-majority eastern province, separate from the western part in which Calcutta, the centre of nationalist activity, lay
The order was issued under the Viceroy, Lord Curzon, in July 1905

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The division created a Muslim-majority eastern province, separate from the western part in which Calcutta, the centre of nationalist activity, lay. A size argument cannot explain why the line was drawn so as to make a Muslim-majority eastern province and to separate it from Calcutta, where nationalist opinion was strongest; this is the evidence for "divide and rule". The other three are true but neutral details that fit the administrative reason equally well.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Calcutta shopkeeper who protested in 1905 says at the end of 1911, "Our long campaign has won, yet our city has lost something." Which pair of announcements made at the Delhi Durbar would make both halves of his remark true?

options.text_md: The partition was confirmed, and the capital of British India was to move from Calcutta to Delhi
The partition was annulled, and the Congress was banned in Bengal
The partition was annulled, and the capital of British India was to move from Calcutta to Delhi
The partition was annulled, and Calcutta was to remain the capital with greater powers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The partition was annulled, and the capital of British India was to move from Calcutta to Delhi. His gain is the annulment of the partition in 1911, 6 years after it came into effect; his loss is Calcutta giving up its place as capital to Delhi, announced at the same Durbar. Confirming the partition would not be a victory, the Congress was not banned in Bengal, and Calcutta did not keep the capital.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** 16 October 1905 was observed in Bengal as a day of mourning.

**Reason (R):** Nationalists regarded the partition, which took effect that day, as an attack on the unity of Bengal.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: because the partition took effect that day and was seen as dividing Bengal, people fasted and mourned.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Partition of Bengal led to the Swadeshi and Boycott Movement.

**Reason (R):** Lord Curzon was Viceroy of India from 1899 to 1905.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. The movement arose because people protested against the partition; the dates of Curzon's term do not explain why they adopted swadeshi and boycott.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Indian National Congress welcomed the Partition of Bengal as a useful administrative reform.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The Congress and nationalists across India opposed it as a move to divide Bengal and weaken nationalism.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the stated reason and the nationalist view of the Partition of Bengal.
questions.solution_md: Official reason versus nationalist view.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Stated reason:** Bengal was too **large and populous** to administer efficiently.
**Nationalist view:** it was a policy of **divide and rule**, meant to weaken **Bengali nationalism** and divide **Hindus and Muslims**.

questions.stem_md: Mention two ways in which the people of Bengal showed their opposition to the partition in 1905.
questions.solution_md: Any two forms of protest.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **16 October 1905** was observed as a **day of mourning**, with fasting and closed shops.
2. People took up **swadeshi** and **boycotted British goods**; Hindus and Muslims tied **rakhis** on one another as a sign of unity.

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways in which the Partition of Bengal changed the course of the national movement.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct effects.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It started the **Swadeshi and Boycott Movement**, which drew in **students, women and traders**.
2. It strengthened the **Assertive Nationalists**, since petitions had clearly failed to stop the partition.
3. It spread protest **beyond Bengal** to Maharashtra and Punjab, giving the movement an **all-India** character.

questions.stem_md: The split in the Indian National Congress between the Moderates and the Assertive Nationalists took place at Surat in which year?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 1907. The Surat Split occurred in December 1907, 22 years after the Congress was founded. 1905 was the partition, 1911 its annulment and 1916 the year the two groups came together again at Lucknow.

questions.stem_md: Whom did the Moderates support as President of the Surat session of 1907?

options.text_md: Lala Lajpat Rai
Bal Gangadhar Tilak
Dadabhai Naoroji
Rash Behari Ghosh

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Rash Behari Ghosh. The Moderates backed Rash Behari Ghosh, while the Assertive group wanted Lala Lajpat Rai (or Tilak) to preside. Naoroji had presided in 1906.

questions.stem_md: What was the deeper cause of the Surat Split?

options.text_md: Disagreement over the language in which the session would be held
Disagreement over goals and methods: the Assertive group wanted to keep swadeshi, boycott and national education, which many Moderates wished to limit
A dispute about who would pay for the session
A disagreement about whether to admit members from Madras

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Disagreement over goals and methods: the Assertive group wanted to keep swadeshi, boycott and national education, which many Moderates wished to limit. The real issue was methods and goals: the Assertive Nationalists wanted to continue the 1906 resolutions on swadeshi, boycott and national education, while many Moderates wanted to soften them. The other options are not the cause.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student lists four developments as reasons why the Moderates and the Assertive group could come together again at Lucknow in 1916. One of them cannot be a reason, because of its date. Which one?

options.text_md: Lala Lajpat Rai's injury at a demonstration against the Simon Commission, 1928
The annulment of the Partition of Bengal, 1911
Tilak's release from Mandalay, 1914
The weakening of the Congress after the Surat Split, 1907

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Lala Lajpat Rai's injury at a demonstration against the Simon Commission, 1928. An event can only help explain a reunion if it came before it. The Simon Commission demonstration of 1928 was twelve years after Lucknow, so it cannot be a reason. The annulment of the partition (1911), Tilak's return from prison (1914) and the weakness the split had caused (from 1907) all came earlier.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Congress session of 1907 had first been planned for Nagpur but was held at Surat.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The venue was moved from Nagpur, a centre of Assertive support, to Surat, which was widely seen as favouring the Moderates.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events of the national movement in the order in which they happened.

options.text_md: Tilak starts a Home Rule League
The Partition of Bengal comes into effect
The partition is annulled
The Congress splits at Surat

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Partition (1905) → Surat Split (1907) → annulment (1911) → Home Rule League (1916).

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons for the split in the Congress at Surat in 1907.
questions.solution_md: Methods; presidency dispute.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Differences over methods:** the Assertive group wanted to extend **swadeshi, boycott and passive resistance**, while the Moderates preferred **constitutional** methods.
2. **Dispute over the presidency:** the Moderates backed **Rash Behari Ghosh**; the Assertive group wanted **Lala Lajpat Rai**, and the session broke up in disorder.

questions.stem_md: How did the Surat Split affect the Congress in the years that followed?
questions.solution_md: Weakened Congress; reunion only in 1916.

answer.model_answer_md: The Congress was left in the hands of the **Moderates**, and the Assertive leaders were outside it, so it became **weaker** and less active. The government also **arrested** leading Assertive Nationalists, and unity returned only at **Lucknow in 1916**.

questions.stem_md: What was the main political goal of the Assertive Nationalists?

options.text_md: More seats for Europeans in the councils
Swaraj, or self-rule
Only lower salt prices
A return to Mughal rule

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Swaraj, or self-rule. The Assertive Nationalists made swaraj (self-rule) their goal. The other options are not their aims.

questions.stem_md: What did the term "swadeshi" mean in the movement of 1905?

options.text_md: Refusing to pay all taxes
Joining the British army
Using goods made in one's own country
Travelling abroad for education

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Using goods made in one's own country. Swadeshi meant using goods made in India, which encouraged Indian industry. It did not mean tax refusal, army service or study abroad.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined Calcutta market of 1906, students picket shops that still sell Manchester cloth, and the same students raise money for a handloom workshop that will supply cloth made in Bengal. Why would Assertive leaders want both activities together?

options.text_md: Picketing was lawful but the workshop was a form of armed resistance
The workshop would sell cloth in Britain to repay the drain of wealth
Both were meant to persuade Parliament to pass a law, in the manner of the Moderates
Boycott pressed British trade while swadeshi supplied Indian goods in its place, so the two supported each other

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Boycott pressed British trade while swadeshi supplied Indian goods in its place, so the two supported each other. Boycott alone would leave buyers without cloth; swadeshi alone would not pressure British trade. Together they hurt foreign trade and built Indian industry. A workshop is not armed resistance, the aim was not to export to Britain, and appealing to Parliament was the Moderate way, not theirs.

questions.stem_md: Why did the Assertive Nationalists set up national schools and colleges?

options.text_md: To train students only for the British civil service
To replace all schools with religious seminaries
To teach only in English and stop the use of Indian languages
To give education that built national pride and was free from government control

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** To give education that built national pride and was free from government control. National education aimed to build self-reliance and national pride, with teaching partly in Indian languages and outside official control. It was not meant only to supply the civil service, was not purely religious, and did not abolish Indian languages.

questions.stem_md: Which event outside India encouraged Indian nationalists after 1905 by showing that an Asian nation could defeat a European power?

options.text_md: The French Revolution, 1789
The end of the First World War, 1918
Japan's victory over Russia, 1905
The American Civil War, 1861–65

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Japan's victory over Russia, 1905. Japan's victory over Russia in 1905 boosted Asian self-confidence and is often listed among the causes of the rise of the Assertive Nationalists. The other events are unrelated in time or meaning.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly contrasts the two groups in the Congress?

options.text_md: The Moderates wanted swaraj at once; the Assertive Nationalists wanted only small reforms
The Moderates relied on petitions; the Assertive Nationalists relied on swadeshi, boycott and passive resistance
Both groups used armed revolt as their main method
Both groups refused to take part in any public meetings

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Moderates relied on petitions; the Assertive Nationalists relied on swadeshi, boycott and passive resistance. The Moderates worked through petitions and appeals, while the Assertive Nationalists used swadeshi, boycott, national education and passive resistance. The second option reverses the groups, and the last two are false.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Swadeshi Movement helped Indian industries such as textile mills and match factories.

**Reason (R):** Boycott of foreign goods increased the demand for goods made in India.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: when people stopped buying British goods, demand for Indian products rose, helping Indian industries.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Assertive Nationalists wanted ordinary people to take part in the national movement.

**Reason (R):** The Assertive Nationalists believed that petitions to the British Parliament were the best way to win swaraj.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true: they sought wider popular participation. R is false: they had lost faith in petitions and preferred swadeshi, boycott and passive resistance.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Passive resistance, as used by the Assertive Nationalists, meant refusing to cooperate with unjust government measures without using violence.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Passive resistance meant peaceful non-cooperation with unjust laws and measures.

questions.stem_md: The Assertive Nationalists made ___ (self-rule) the goal of the national movement.
questions.solution_md: Their goal was swaraj, or self-rule.

questions.stem_md: Mention any two methods of struggle adopted by the Assertive Nationalists.
questions.solution_md: Any two Assertive methods.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Swadeshi**: using Indian-made goods and supporting Indian industry.
2. **Boycott** of foreign goods, and also of government schools, courts and titles. (Also: national education, passive resistance.)

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons for the rise of the Assertive Nationalists around 1905.
questions.solution_md: Any two causes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Failure of Moderate methods:** years of petitions had brought few results.
2. **Repressive policies of Lord Curzon**, especially the **Partition of Bengal**, and outside events such as **Japan's victory over Russia (1905)** that built confidence.

questions.stem_md: What was meant by national education, and why did the Assertive Nationalists support it?
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus purpose.

answer.model_answer_md: **National education** meant schools and colleges run by **Indians**, outside government control, that taught **pride in India** and practical skills. They supported it to free young minds from a **colonial outlook** and to build **self-reliance**.

questions.stem_md: Compare the Early Nationalists and the Assertive Nationalists on any three points.
questions.solution_md: Three points of comparison, each with both sides.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Goal:** the Early Nationalists sought **reforms within British rule**; the Assertive Nationalists demanded **swaraj**.
2. **Methods:** petitions, prayers and protests against **swadeshi, boycott and passive resistance**.
3. **Base of support:** the **educated middle class** against wider **popular participation**, including students and women.

marking_scheme.step: Support base or attitude to British rule

questions.stem_md: Bal Gangadhar Tilak ran which two newspapers?

options.text_md: Kesari and Mahratta
The Bengalee and Amrita Bazar Patrika
New India and Young India
The Hindu and The Tribune

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Kesari and Mahratta. Tilak ran Kesari (Marathi) and Mahratta (English). The Bengalee was Banerjee's; the other pairs are unrelated to Tilak.

questions.stem_md: Why did Tilak turn the Ganapati and Shivaji festivals into public celebrations?

options.text_md: To raise money for the British government
To bring ordinary people together and spread national feeling through popular gatherings
To replace the Indian National Congress
To stop the use of the Marathi language

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** To bring ordinary people together and spread national feeling through popular gatherings. Public festivals let Tilak reach ordinary people and build pride and unity. They did not raise money for the government, did not replace the Congress, and promoted rather than suppressed Marathi.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student writes: "Tilak was freed from Mandalay in 1914 and started his Home Rule League in 1916, so the League was a protest against the Partition of Bengal." Which correction is best?

options.text_md: The League was started before his release, so the sequence must be reversed
The League was started in 1907, straight after the Surat Split, so it was a protest against the split
Tilak was never imprisoned at Mandalay, so his dates are wrong
The partition had been annulled in 1911, so the League of 1916 pressed a wider demand for self-government instead

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The partition had been annulled in 1911, so the League of 1916 pressed a wider demand for self-government instead. The student has taken the order of events as proof of a cause. The partition was annulled in 1911, five years before the League, and the League demanded self-government, so the cause cannot be the partition. The other options contradict the dates: release (1914) came before the League (1916), the League was not started in 1907, and Tilak was imprisoned at Mandalay (1908–14).

questions.stem_md: Tilak is widely remembered for declaring that self-rule was an Indian's birthright which he would claim. Which idea does this declaration express?

options.text_md: Swaraj is a natural right of Indians, not a favour to be granted by the British
Indians should seek only small reforms within British rule
Indians should leave politics to the British
Self-rule should be postponed for a hundred years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Swaraj is a natural right of Indians, not a favour to be granted by the British. The declaration, described here in our own words, treats swaraj as a right Indians possess, not a concession. The other options contradict it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined editorial in a Calcutta weekly of 1906 says that its writer will send no more petitions, and urges readers to stop buying foreign cloth, to leave official schools and to build institutions of their own. Which reading of the editorial is best?

options.text_md: It is Moderate, because it asks the British to hear the case of Indians
It is Assertive, because it calls for armed attack on government offices
It is Assertive, because it replaces petitions with refusal and self-reliance
It is Moderate, because boycott had been the Moderate method since 1885

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It is Assertive, because it replaces petitions with refusal and self-reliance. Giving up petitions, boycotting foreign cloth, leaving official schools and building national institutions are the marks of the Assertive programme of swadeshi, boycott and national education, as argued by leaders such as Bipin Chandra Pal. Nothing in it asks the British to hear a case, it proposes no armed attack, and boycott was not a Moderate method.

questions.stem_md: Which Assertive Nationalist leader came to be called "Punjab Kesari" (the Lion of Punjab)?

options.text_md: Bipin Chandra Pal
Gopal Krishna Gokhale
Lala Lajpat Rai
Surendranath Banerjee

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Lala Lajpat Rai. Lala Lajpat Rai was known as Punjab Kesari. Pal was from Bengal, and Gokhale and Banerjee were Moderates.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Lahore newspaper of 1907 reports that a popular leader has been deported without trial after farmers' meetings against new land rules. Which inference about the government's thinking is best supported?

options.text_md: It feared a leader who could rouse ordinary people on everyday grievances, which petitions in the council hall never did
It was punishing him for a petition he had sent to Parliament
It was acting on a request from the Congress after the Surat Split
It had accepted his demand for swaraj and was removing him to a safe place

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It feared a leader who could rouse ordinary people on everyday grievances, which petitions in the council hall never did. Deportation without trial, following mass meetings of farmers, shows alarm at popular agitation of the Assertive kind (the leader was Lala Lajpat Rai, who was deported to Mandalay in 1907). A petition to Parliament was a Moderate, lawful method and would not be punished so, the Congress made no such request, and the government had not accepted swaraj.

questions.stem_md: The trio of Assertive leaders popularly called "Lal, Bal and Pal" stood for which three leaders?

options.text_md: Lal Bahadur Shastri, Balwant Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal
Lala Lajpat Rai, Balasaheb Kher and Pherozeshah Mehta
Lal Mohan Ghosh, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Gopal Krishna Gokhale
Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal. Lal, Bal and Pal were Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal, the leading Assertive Nationalists of Punjab, Maharashtra and Bengal.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Bal Gangadhar Tilak was a leader of the Early Nationalists who opposed boycott and swadeshi.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Tilak was a leading Assertive Nationalist who strongly supported swadeshi, boycott and national education.

questions.stem_md: Tilak's Marathi newspaper was called ___.
questions.solution_md: Tilak's Marathi paper was Kesari; his English paper was Mahratta.

questions.stem_md: State two contributions of Bal Gangadhar Tilak to the national movement.
questions.solution_md: Any two contributions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Through **Kesari** and **Mahratta** he spread the demand for **swaraj** and criticised government policy.
2. He organised the **Ganapati** and **Shivaji festivals** to unite people, and started a **Home Rule League in 1916**.

questions.stem_md: State two contributions of Bipin Chandra Pal.
questions.solution_md: Any two contributions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He spread nationalist ideas through his English weekly **New India** and other writing.
2. He was a leading speaker of the **Swadeshi Movement** in Bengal, urging **boycott** and **national education**.

questions.stem_md: State two contributions of Lala Lajpat Rai.
questions.solution_md: Any two contributions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He led the **Swadeshi** and protest movement in **Punjab** and was **deported to Mandalay in 1907**.
2. Linked with the **Arya Samaj**, he worked for **education** and public causes; known as **Punjab Kesari**, he was one of the trio **Lal, Bal and Pal**.

questions.stem_md: How did Lal, Bal and Pal together give the Assertive movement an all-India character? Give three points.
questions.solution_md: Regions; means of reaching people; common programme.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Each led the movement in a **different region**: **Punjab** (Lajpat Rai), **Maharashtra** (Tilak) and **Bengal** (Pal).
2. They used **newspapers** in several languages and **public meetings** to reach ordinary people.
3. They spread the same programme of **swaraj, swadeshi and boycott** across these regions, so the movement was not confined to Bengal.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the first phase of the Congress.

(i) State three objectives of the Early Nationalists. **[3]**
(ii) Describe three methods they used. **[3]**
(iii) Give two achievements and two limitations of the Early Nationalists. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Objectives; methods; balanced appraisal.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Expansion of legislative councils** with more elected Indians; **Indianisation of services** (civil service examination in India too); **economic reforms** such as lower land revenue and less military spending (also civil rights such as a free Press).

(ii) **Petitions and memoranda** to the government; **public meetings and resolutions** to build opinion; **delegations** and appeals to British leaders and voters, trusting in British justice.

(iii) **Achievements:** they built an **all-India platform** and political awareness, and exposed **economic exploitation**; the **Indian Councils Act, 1892** answered some demands. **Limitations:** their support was mainly the **educated middle class**, and **petitions** brought only small results.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about three Early Nationalist leaders.

(i) State the contributions of Dadabhai Naoroji. **[3]**
(ii) State the contributions of Surendranath Banerjee. **[3]**
(iii) State the contributions of Gopal Krishna Gokhale and explain why he was respected by later leaders. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Contributions of each leader.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) He set out the **drain of wealth** argument; was elected to the **House of Commons (1892)** and raised Indian issues there; was **Congress President** in **1886, 1893 and 1906**.

(ii) He founded the **Indian Association (1876)**; led an all-India campaign on the **civil service age limit**; edited **The Bengalee** and led protests against the **Partition of Bengal**.

(iii) He founded the **Servants of India Society (1905)**; presided over the **Banaras session (1905)**; in the **Imperial Legislative Council** he criticised budgets with facts and figures. He was respected for **honesty, careful argument** and devotion to **public service**, and **Gandhi** regarded him as his political guide.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the Partition of Bengal.

(i) When and under which Viceroy was Bengal partitioned, and what new province was created? **[3]**
(ii) What reason did the government give, and how did nationalists see the partition? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how people protested against the partition and what the final outcome was. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Facts; reasons and views; protest and outcome.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The partition was announced in **July 1905** and took effect on **16 October 1905**, under **Lord Curzon**. The eastern districts were joined with **Assam** to form **Eastern Bengal and Assam**, with its capital at **Dacca**.

(ii) The government said Bengal was **too large** to govern efficiently. Nationalists saw it as **divide and rule**: an attempt to weaken **Bengali nationalism** and divide **Hindus and Muslims** by creating a Muslim-majority province.

(iii) **16 October** was a **day of mourning**; people tied **rakhis** as a symbol of unity; the **Swadeshi and Boycott Movement** spread, with **students** and **women** taking part and Indian industries gaining. The partition was **annulled in 1911**, announced at the **Delhi Durbar**, and the capital moved to **Delhi**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the Surat Split.

(i) What were the main differences between the two groups in the Congress by 1907? **[3]**
(ii) Describe what happened at Surat in December 1907. **[3]**
(iii) Explain the effects of the split on the national movement up to 1916. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Differences; events at Surat; effects.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Goal:** reforms within British rule against **swaraj**. **Methods:** **petitions** against **swadeshi, boycott and passive resistance**. **Attitude:** faith in **British justice** against loss of that faith.

(ii) The session, first planned for **Nagpur**, was moved to **Surat**. The Moderates proposed **Rash Behari Ghosh** as President, while the Assertive group wanted **Lala Lajpat Rai**; there was also fear that the **1906 resolutions** on swadeshi and boycott would be dropped. The session broke up in **disorder** and the Congress **split**.

(iii) The **Moderates** kept control of the Congress, which became **less active**. The government **repressed** the Assertive leaders: **Tilak** was sent to **Mandalay (1908)**. The national movement lost **unity** until the two groups **reunited at Lucknow in 1916**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the Assertive Nationalists.

(i) State three causes of the rise of the Assertive Nationalists. **[3]**
(ii) State their objectives. **[3]**
(iii) Explain the methods of swadeshi, boycott and national education. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Causes; objectives; three methods explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Failure of Moderate methods:** twenty years of petitions had won only small reforms. **Lord Curzon's policies**, above all the **Partition of Bengal**, showed that the government ignored Indian opinion. **Japan's victory over Russia (1905)** proved that an Asian people could defeat a European power and raised self-confidence (economic distress, famine and plague also added to anger).

(ii) **Swaraj** or self-rule as the goal; **mass participation** of ordinary people, not only the educated few; **self-reliance** and pride in Indian culture; an end to dependence on the goodwill of the British.

(iii) **Swadeshi:** using **Indian-made goods**, which helped Indian **industries** such as textile mills. **Boycott:** refusing **British goods**, and also government **schools, courts and titles**, so that British trade and authority were hurt. **National education:** schools and colleges run by Indians outside **government control**, teaching in Indian languages and building **national pride** and practical skills.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about three Assertive Nationalist leaders.

(i) State three contributions of Bal Gangadhar Tilak. **[3]**
(ii) State three contributions of Bipin Chandra Pal. **[3]**
(iii) State four contributions of Lala Lajpat Rai. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Contributions of each leader.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) He spread the idea of **swaraj** as a **birthright** through **Kesari** and **Mahratta**; organised the **Ganapati and Shivaji festivals** to unite people; started a **Home Rule League (1916)**; suffered imprisonment at **Mandalay (1908–14)**.

(ii) He started the English weekly **New India**; was a leading speaker of the **Swadeshi Movement** in Bengal; urged **boycott** and **national education**.

(iii) He led protests in **Punjab** and was **deported to Mandalay (1907)**; was linked with the **Arya Samaj** and worked for **education**; was called **Punjab Kesari**; formed with Tilak and Pal the trio **Lal, Bal and Pal**. (Later, in **1928**, he was injured during a protest against the **Simon Commission** and died soon after.)

questions.stem_md:
Historians often compare the two early phases of the national movement.

(i) Compare the Early and Assertive Nationalists on goals and methods. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how the work of the Early Nationalists prepared the ground for the Assertive phase. **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate which group did more for the freedom struggle up to 1916, giving reasons for both sides. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Comparison; continuity; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Goals:** reforms within British rule against **swaraj**. **Methods:** **petitions, prayers and protests** against **swadeshi, boycott, national education and passive resistance**.

(ii) The Moderates built an **all-India organisation**, spread **political awareness**, and exposed **economic exploitation** through the **drain** argument; when their methods failed to stop the **partition**, younger leaders built on this awareness with stronger methods.

(iii) **For the Moderates:** they laid the **foundation**, trained leaders, and won early reforms such as the **1892 Act**. **For the Assertive group:** they gave the movement **mass support**, a clear goal of **swaraj** and methods that hit British trade. A balanced judgement may hold that each was **necessary**: the Assertive phase grew on Moderate foundations. Any reasoned conclusion earns credit.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **1905: Partition of Bengal**, under **Lord Curzon**, effective 16 October. **1907: Surat Split**, the Congress divided over methods and the presidency. **1911: annulment** of the partition, announced at the **Delhi Durbar**.

(ii) **1876: Indian Association**, founded by **Surendranath Banerjee** and Ananda Mohan Bose. **1892: Dadabhai Naoroji** elected to the **House of Commons**, where he raised Indian issues.

(iii) In **1905** the partition set off **swadeshi and boycott** and raised the **Assertive** leaders; in **1906** **swaraj** was declared the goal at Calcutta; the **Surat Split (1907)** divided and weakened the Congress; the **annulment (1911)** showed that mass protest could work; by **1916** the **Home Rule League** marked a new, more popular phase.
